instruction_head:
I need a high-performance embedded key-value storage engine built in Go from scratch, using an LSM-Tree (Log-Structured Merge-Tree) architecture with full MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) support, optimistic transactions, and advanced query capabilities. The engine must be accessible through a command-line interface that reads commands from stdin (one per line) and writes results to stdout.

behavior_constraints: PUT --ttl <seconds> sets key to expire that many seconds after write time (wall-clock Unix seconds)
GET on an expired key returns NOT_FOUND
SCAN excludes expired keys from results
Compaction may GC expired keys but must respect MVCC snapshot visibility — a snapshot taken before the expiration timestamp still sees the key
TTL <key> returns remaining seconds until expiration as an integer rounded down, -1 if the key has no TTL, or NOT_FOUND if the key does not exist
PUT without --ttl on a key that previously had a TTL clears the TTL
TX_PUT and BATCH PUT accept --ttl <seconds>
STATS includes expired_keys (count of keys whose TTL elapsed but not yet GC'd) and total_keys must exclude expired keys
WAL single entry format: expire_at (uint64 LE, Unix seconds, 0 = no expiration) immediately after seqnum
WAL batch op format: op (uint8) + expire_at (uint64 LE) + key_len (uint32 LE) + key + val_len (uint32 LE) + value

instruction_head:
I need key expiration support. Add a `--ttl <seconds>` flag to `PUT` — when set, the key expires after that many seconds from the time of the write (use wall-clock time). Expired keys behave exactly like deleted keys: `GET` returns `NOT_FOUND`, `SCAN` excludes them, and compaction can GC them (respecting MVCC snapshot visibility — a snapshot taken before expiration still sees the key).

behavior_constraints: L0-to-L1 compaction must retain key versions still visible to active MVCC snapshots; after such compaction, snapshots must not return NOT_FOUND for keys whose versions existed at snapshot time.
Full compaction behavior for snapshot visibility must remain correct and unchanged.
Every SSTable data block must be followed by a 4-byte little-endian CRC-32 (IEEE) checksum of the block's raw bytes.
SSTable index entry block_size must exclude the trailing checksum bytes.
SSTable reader must verify each data block checksum on read and return 'ERROR: data corruption detected' on mismatch.
VERIFY command must scan every SSTable file in the data directory and validate footer magic, all data block checksums, bloom filter integrity, and index integrity.
VERIFY must print 'OK' if all files are clean; otherwise print 'CORRUPT: <filename> (<reason>)' per corrupt file and a final 'VERIFY_FAILED: <N> file(s) corrupted'.

instruction_head:
Two things this round.

First, there's a snapshot bug: if you write a bunch of keys, take a snapshot, write new versions of those keys, and enough flushes happen to trigger the L0-to-L1 compaction, the snapshot starts returning `NOT_FOUND` for keys it should still see. The full compaction path handles this correctly, so it's just the L0 compaction that's dropping versions it shouldn't. Fix that.

Second, add data block checksums to SSTables. Each data block should be followed by a CRC-32 (IEEE)

behavior_constraints: MERGE <key> <operand> appends operand to the key's value as a comma-separated list and outputs 'OK <seqnum>'
If key does not exist or was deleted, MERGE makes the operand the sole value
Multiple MERGEs stack: MERGE k a; MERGE k b; MERGE k c => GET k returns 'a,b,c'
PUT k x; MERGE k y; MERGE k z => GET k returns 'x,y,z'
MERGE entries use op_type 4 in WAL and SSTable records, storing the operand in the value field

Read path (GET, SCAN, snapshot reads, transaction reads) collects all MERGE entries for a key back to the most recent PUT or DELETE (or start of history) and folds them left-to-right with comma joining
TX_MERGE <tx_id> <key> <operand> and BATCH MERGE <key> <operand> behave identically to MERGE
During compaction, a run of MERGE entries for the same key collapses into a single entry only if no open snapshot needs the intermediate states
A run of MERGEs with no preceding PUT compacts into a single PUT whose value is the folded comma-joined result
STATS reports merge_operations = total number of uncompacted MERGE entries across the memtable and all SSTables

instruction_head: Add a merge operator. New command: `MERGE <key> <operand>` — appends the operand to the key's value as a comma-separated list. If the key already has a value from a previous PUT or MERGE, the new operand is appended with a comma separator. If the key doesn't exist or was deleted, the operand becomes the sole value. behavior_constraints: CURSOR_OPEN creates a cursor over a snapshot taken at open time and outputs CURSOR:<id> with id monotonically increasing from 1; the cursor starts before the first key in its active direction.

--prefix

restricts the cursor to keys with that prefix; --reverse swaps CURSOR_NEXT and CURSOR_PREV directions.
CURSOR_NEXT advances one position in the cursor direction and outputs <key>	<value>, or END if exhausted.
CURSOR_PREV moves one position opposite to the cursor direction and outputs <key>	<value>, or END if before the first key in the active direction.

CURSOR_SEEK positions at the smallest key >= seek key, or largest key <= seek key when --reverse, outputs <key>	<value> or END; after seek, CURSOR_NEXT advances from the seeked position and CURSOR_PREV returns the key before the seeked position.
CURSOR_CLOSE outputs OK and releases the cursor and its underlying snapshot.
Operations on invalid cursor IDs return ERROR: invalid cursor.
Cursors see a consistent snapshot view: expired, deleted, and range-tombstoned keys are invisible.
Merged keys return their folded merge value from the R4 read path.
STATS includes open_cursors.

instruction_head:
Add server-side cursors. `CURSOR_OPEN [flags]` creates a cursor backed by a snapshot taken at open time. Output: `CURSOR:` where id is a monotonically increasing integer starting at 1. The cursor starts positioned *before* the first key. Flags: `--prefix

` restricts the cursor to keys with that prefix, `--reverse` flips the direction so CURSOR_NEXT goes backward and CURSOR_PREV goes forward. `CURSOR_NEXT ` — advance one position, output `\t`, or `END` if exhausted.

behavior_constraints: WAL is stored as numbered segment files wal_000001.log, wal_000002.log, ... in the data directory instead of a single file
A new WAL segment is started when the current segment reaches or exceeds 64KB
On memtable flush, all WAL segments whose highest seqnum is <= the flushed seqnum are deleted
The active WAL segment is not truncated or deleted on memtable flush
On startup, all WAL segment files are replayed in numerical order
Per-segment CRC rules apply; a corrupted entry stops replay of that segment and all later segments are skipped entirely
CURSOR_SEEK to an existing key positions the cursor so an immediate CURSOR_PREV returns the key before the seeked key (e.g., PUT a,b,c,d; SEEK c returns c; PREV returns b, not c again)

BACKUP creates a consistent point-in-time copy of all current SSTable files into the given directory
backup.meta contains a header line `max_seqnum=<N>` where N is the global max seqnum at backup time
backup.meta contains one line per SSTable formatted as `<filename> <level> <max_seqnum>`

RESTORE <path> clears the entire current data directory (SSTables, WAL segments, everything)
RESTORE copies the backed-up SSTables into the data directory

instruction_head: Add online backup and restore. `BACKUP <path>` flushes the current memtable to disk, then creates a consistent point-in-time copy of the database at the given directory path. The backup contains copies of all current SSTable files plus a `backup.meta` file listing each SSTable filename, its level, and the max sequence number at backup time — one line per SSTable as `<filename> <level> <max_seqnum>`, with a header line `max_seqnum=<N>` where N is the global max seqnum. No WAL files in the backup.
